id: How to Write a Poem in a Time of War

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

You can’t begin just anywhere. It’s a wreck. Shrapnel and the eye Of a house, a row of houses. There’s a rat scrambling From light with fleshy trash in its mouth. A baby strapped to its mother’s back Cut loose. Soldiers crawl the city, The river, the town, the village, The bedroom, our kitchen. They eat everything. Or burn it. They kill what they cannot take. They rape. What they cannot kill they take. Rumors fall like rain. Like bombs. Like mother and father tears swallowed for restless peace. Like sunset slanting toward a moonless midnight. Like a train blown free of its destination. Like a seed fallen where There is no chance of trees or anyplace for birds to live.No, start here. Deer peer from the edge of the woods. We used to see woodpeckers The size of the sun, redbirds, and were greeted By chickadees with their good morning songs. We’d started to cook outside slippery with dew and laughter, ah those smoky sweet sunrises. We tried to pretend war wasn’t going to happen. Though they began building their houses all around us and demanding more. They started teaching our children their god’s story, A story in which we’d always be slaves.No. Not here. You can’t begin here. This is memory shredded because it is impossible to hold by words, even poetry.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The poem depicts the brutal devastation of war, showing destroyed homes, scavenging rats, and civilians like a mother and baby caught in the violence.
- Invading soldiers ravage every space from cities to kitchens, killing, raping, burning, and taking whatever they cannot destroy.
- Pervasive rumors and fear fall like rain and bombs, conveying the relentless anxiety and dread that saturate life during wartime.
- The speaker contrasts the horror with peaceful memories of nature and community, recalling woodpeckers, birdsong, and joyful outdoor cooking before the war arrived.
- The invaders imposed their culture and religion on the people, teaching their children a god's story that cast them permanently as slaves.
- The poem struggles with the impossibility of narrating trauma, as memory is too shredded and painful to be contained even by poetry.

outputs.L1:
You can't begin just anywhere. It's a wreck.
Shrapnel and the vacant eye
Of a house, a row of houses.
There's a rat scrambling
From the light with fleshy trash in its mouth.
A baby, strapped to its mother's back,
Cut loose.
Soldiers crawl through the city,
The river, the town, the village,
The bedroom, our kitchen.
They devour everything.
Or set it ablaze.
They kill what they cannot carry away.
They rape. What they cannot kill, they seize.
Rumors fall like rain.
Like bombs.
Like a mother's and father's tears swallowed for the sake of a restless peace.
Like sunset slanting toward a moonless midnight.
Like a train torn free of its destination.
Like a seed fallen where
There is no hope of trees, nor any place for birds to nest.

No, begin here.
Deer peer out from the edge of the woods.
We used to see woodpeckers
As vast as the sun, and cardinals, and were greeted
By chickadees singing their good-morning songs.
We had begun to cook outside, slick with dew and laughter—
ah, those smoky, sweet sunrises.
We tried to pretend that war would never come.
Though they began raising their houses all around us, demanding ever more.
They set about teaching our children their god's story,
A story in which we would forever remain slaves.

No. Not here. You cannot begin here.
This is memory shredded, because it is impossible to hold
within words—even poetry.
outputs.L2:
There's no proper place to start. Everything lies in ruins. Fragments of metal and the hollowed socket of a home, then house after house. A rat darts away from the light, dragging bloody scraps between its teeth. An infant, once bound to its mother's back, has been torn away. Soldiers creep through every place—the city, the flowing river, the town, the little village, the bedroom, even the kitchen where we cook. Everything gets devoured. Or set aflame. Whatever they can't carry off, they destroy. They violate bodies. Whatever survives, they seize.

Gossip pours down endlessly. Like a downpour. Like falling explosives. Like the tears of parents choked back for the sake of a fragile calm. Like the sun sinking into a darkness without any moon. Like a train scattered apart before it ever reaches where it's going. Like a seed that lands somewhere barren, where no tree will ever grow and no bird will ever find a home.

No—let me begin over here instead. Deer look out cautiously from where the forest ends. Once, we spotted woodpeckers as enormous as the sun, along with cardinals, and the chickadees would welcome us with their cheerful morning tunes. We had taken up cooking in the open air, everything wet with dew and filled with laughter—oh, those hazy, sweet mornings when the sun came up. We did our best to imagine the war would never arrive. Yet all the while, they kept constructing their homes surrounding us and kept demanding still more. They set about instructing our children in the tale of their god—a tale that forever cast us as slaves.

No. Not this place either. You cannot start here. These are memories torn to pieces, because words can't contain them—not even poems can.
outputs.L3:
# The Devastation of War: An Analysis

The poem offers a harrowing portrayal of war's brutal devastation, painting a landscape of ruin where homes lie destroyed and rats scavenge through the wreckage. Amid this desolation, the human cost becomes painfully visible through the image of civilians—a mother and her baby—caught helplessly in the violence that surrounds them. These figures embody the innocent lives shattered by conflict, grounding the poem's larger themes in intimate, personal suffering.

The invading soldiers move through every space imaginable, from sprawling cities down to the private intimacy of kitchens. Nothing remains untouched by their presence. They kill, rape, and burn without mercy, and whatever they cannot destroy outright, they take as plunder. This relentless invasion of both public and domestic spheres emphasizes how war violates not only nations but the most personal corners of everyday life.

Throughout the poem, rumors and fear become pervasive forces, falling like rain and bombs upon the population. This imagery captures the relentless anxiety and dread that saturate existence during wartime. The comparison to natural and mechanical downpours suggests that fear is both inescapable and constant, an atmosphere in which people are forced to live and breathe.

Against this backdrop of horror, the speaker draws a poignant contrast with peaceful memories of the past. Recollections of nature and community surface—the sound of woodpeckers, the melody of birdsong, and the simple joy of cooking outdoors among loved ones. These tender images of life before the war heighten the tragedy by reminding us of everything that has been lost, offering a glimpse of the ordinary beauty that violence has stolen away.

The poem also addresses the cultural and spiritual dimensions of oppression. The invaders imposed their own culture and religion upon the conquered people, teaching their children a god's story crafted to cast them permanently in the role of slaves. This detail reveals how conquest extends beyond physical destruction into the realm of identity and belief, seeking to reshape a people's understanding of themselves and their place in the world.

Finally, the poem grapples with the profound difficulty of narrating trauma. Memory itself proves too shredded and painful to be fully contained, even within the structured vessel of poetry. This struggle reflects a central paradox: the very act of bearing witness to atrocity strains against the limits of language and form. In acknowledging this impossibility, the poem conveys the depth of suffering that resists articulation, leaving readers to confront the silences and fractures that trauma leaves behind.
outputs.L4:
# The Impossibility of Narration: War, Trauma, and the Failure of Poetic Form

This poem grapples with the fundamental impossibility of narrating war and displacement, using fragmented imagery and repeated false starts to convey the profound trauma of violence, occupation, and cultural erasure. Rather than presenting a linear account of catastrophe, the poem enacts the very difficulty it describes—the way in which extreme suffering resists being organized into coherent language. Each attempt to construct a narrative breaks down, and these breakdowns are not failures of technique but deliberate demonstrations of how trauma disrupts our conventional understanding of storytelling.

## The Search for a Beginning

At the heart of the poem lies a struggle to locate a proper starting point. Where does one begin the story of a devastated homeland or a shattered people? The poem first reaches toward destruction itself as an origin—the rubble, the violence, the moment of rupture that seems to demand acknowledgment. Yet this beginning proves inadequate, for destruction is not truly a beginning but an ending, a consequence of forces that preceded it.

The poem then shifts, retreating instead into idyllic memory: images of a life before catastrophe, a landscape unmarred, a culture intact. But this beginning also collapses under its own weight. To begin in remembered beauty is to court a nostalgia that cannot survive contact with what came after. The peaceful past becomes unbearable precisely because we know its fate, and so this starting point, too, fails to hold.

## Fragmentation as Meaning

The poem's fractured structure—its shifting attempts, its refusals to settle—is not incidental but essential to its meaning. By offering us false start after false start, the poem reveals that certain kinds of suffering cannot be smoothed into narrative sequence. The violence of occupation and the erasure of a culture do not follow the tidy logic of beginning, middle, and end. They leave behind only shredded memory, fragments that will not cohere into a whole.

In this way, the poem performs a kind of honest inadequacy. It demonstrates that even poetry—that art form most often praised for its capacity to give shape to the unspeakable—ultimately fails to contain the full weight of catastrophe. This failure, however, becomes its own form of testimony. By showing us the limits of expression, the poem bears witness to a suffering so vast that it exceeds the reach of language itself.

## Conclusion

Ultimately, the poem's power lies in its refusal to pretend that coherence is possible. Through its restless movement between destruction and memory, its accumulation of broken images, and its acknowledgment of its own insufficiency, it honors the reality of trauma more faithfully than any seamless account could. It reminds us that some catastrophes cannot be narrated—only gestured toward, circled, and mourned in the very act of failing to speak them whole.
outputs.L5:
# The Weight of What Remains

**You** never expected the world to change in a single heartbeat. One moment you were laughing at something small and forgettable, and the next, the air itself seemed to fracture around you. That's how it happens—no warning, no gentle transition, just the sudden collapse of everything ordinary.

**Shrapnel** has a way of scattering not just metal, but memory. It lodges itself into places you didn't know were vulnerable. The physical fragments, doctors can remove; they can trace the pathways of damage and repair what tools allow. But there are other kinds of shrapnel—the words spoken in anger, the losses that arrive without ceremony, the sharp edges of grief that embed themselves in the soft tissue of who you are. These pieces stay. They migrate. Sometimes years later, they surface again, catching you off guard when you least expect it.

**There** is always a place you're trying to reach—a version of peace, a sense of wholeness, a moment before everything shattered. You point toward it like a distant shore. *There*, you tell yourself, *is where I'll finally feel whole again.* But healing rarely works in straight lines. The journey bends and doubles back. Some days you feel close, and other days the horizon seems to retreat entirely.

And yet, you keep walking.

Because that's what survival demands—not the absence of scars, but the willingness to carry them forward. The shrapnel becomes part of your story, not the end of it. And there, somewhere ahead, is the person you're still becoming.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem about war and displacement that keeps interrupting itself, unable to find the right place to begin the story.
counterfactuals.output:
**Where to Begin**

Begin with the house. No—
begin with the door of the house,
the one that no longer opens onto anything.

No. Start earlier.
Start with the morning the radio said a word
we didn't know yet meant *leave.*

That's wrong too. That's already the middle.

Let me try:
There was a country. There were lemons.
My grandmother—

no, not her, not yet, I can't,
her hands come later, if they come at all—

Start with the map, then.
The map is neutral. The map won't cry.
Here is the border, a thin line
somebody drew while drinking coffee,
a line that later learned to bleed—

I'm doing it again. Making it a poem.
It wasn't a poem. It was a Tuesday.

Okay. Facts.
We packed in twenty minutes.
My brother took the wrong bag,
the one with winter coats, in summer,
which turned out—God—

which turned out to be the right bag
by December, but I can't get to December,
I keep getting stuck in the doorway,

the door that no longer opens onto anything,
you see how I keep arriving there,
how every road I take goes back
to the same threshold I can't cross

or can't stop crossing—

Maybe that's the beginning.
Maybe the beginning is that there isn't one,
just a person in a new country
standing at a stranger's door,

holding a key
to a lock
that is now
someone else's smoke.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a free verse poem in the style of Joy Harjo exploring the trauma of colonization and violence against a community.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the River Remembers

There is a place where the water still knows our names,
though the maps have been redrawn a hundred times,
though the fences run like scars across the grandmother earth.

Listen.

My grandmother carried the songs in her mouth
like seeds she was afraid to swallow,
afraid they would take root in a body
they were teaching her to hate.

They came with their god who did not speak our language,
came with papers and promises
thin as the ice that would not hold us,
came with the word *savage*
pressed against our children's foreheads
like a brand, like a blessing turned to curse.

We were the smoke they tried to scatter.
We were the fire they could not name.

Remember the boarding schools
where they cut the braids—
each strand a road home severed,
each strand a story silenced.
The children came back speaking a stranger's tongue,
their eyes gone quiet as winter fields.
Some did not come back at all.
The ground remembers them.
The ground has always remembered.

But listen—

We are the ones the prophecies spoke of,
the ones who would carry the coals
of the old fires through the long dark.

I am made of the mothers who refused,
of the aunties who hid the medicine in their aprons,
of the ones who whispered ceremony
in the space between one heartbeat and the next.

They took the land.
They could not take the way the land takes us back
when we lie down at last in her arms.

They took the language.
But my daughter is learning the words again,
slow as spring, sure as the return of geese
who know the old routes
written in their blood, in their bones,
in the marrow of belonging.

We are still here.

Do you understand what I am telling you?

Through the massacre and the treaty broken,
through the river poisoned and the sacred mountain sold,
through every generation they tried to end us—

*we are still here.*

And the water still knows our names.
And the water is still singing.
And we are teaching our children
how to listen.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem where the speaker struggles to narrate a traumatic memory of invasion, starting over multiple times with "No, start here."
counterfactuals.output:
**No, Start Here**

Let me begin with the morning. The kettle
was whistling. My mother said the word for *hurry*
in the voice she used for ordinary things.

No, start here: the sky was wrong.
Not dark—too bright, a white that hummed,
and then the windows learned a new way to fall.

No—the dog knew first. Before the sound,
before the ground remembered it could move,
he stood in the doorway, refusing to be called.

I keep arranging the furniture of it.
If I place the table here, the door will hold.
If the door holds, my sister is still braiding

her hair in the mirror that has not yet
become a thousand mirrors on the floor.

No, start here, where I can bear it:
the pear tree in the yard, its stubborn fruit,
how one branch reached across the fence

as if to touch the neighbor's house,
the neighbor's house, which in the after-photograph
is not a house but the idea of a house,

a chalk outline of where a house had knelt.

No. I cannot get the order right.
The smoke came before the fire in my telling.
The scream arrives, then the mouth to hold it.

Let me start where the language still works:
we were people. We had a Tuesday.
We had a kettle and a dog and a pear tree

and the ordinary word for *hurry*—

and then the sentence broke,
and I have been standing in the broken place
ever since, saying *here, here, here,*

pointing at the ground
where I keep trying to build the morning back.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poem contrasting the peaceful life before war—deer, woodpeckers, cooking outside—with the horror of soldiers, rape, and destruction.
counterfactuals.output:
# Before the Soldiers Came

The deer stepped soft through morning mist,
their hoofprints pressed in dew,
and woodpeckers kept time above
the world we thought we knew.

We cooked beneath the open sky,
smoke curling toward the pines,
my grandmother would hum old songs
while stirring in the vines.

The children chased the fireflies
until the stars came out,
and every evening ended slow—
no fear, no need to doubt.

*

Then boots arrived where hooves had walked,
and thunder learned to burn.
The woodpeckers went silent, gone,
and did not once return.

The smoke that rose was not from bread
but from our fallen roofs,
and screams replaced the evening songs,
and blood dried on the hoofs.

They took what men should never take,
they broke what breaks a soul—
the girls who chased the fireflies
would never again be whole.

*

The deer will not come back this year.
The ash lies where they stood.
And still I dream of woodpeckers
and mornings understood—

of cooking underneath the sky,
of songs my grandmother knew,
before the soldiers taught us all
what men were made to do.

---

*This poem holds the weight of what so many have endured. If it speaks to something real for you, I hope it offers a small companionship in that.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_4
